analysis.evidence: In מִן הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא יָצָא, “from that land he went out,” מִן introduces the place of departure for יָצָא.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew preposition without a prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: מִן הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא means “from that land.” The demonstrative points back to Shinar in verse 10, identifying the territory from which the departure took place.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הָ־ precedes a common noun of both genders in the singular absolute. The feminine singular demonstrative הַהִוא agrees with the noun here.

analysis.evidence: In מִן הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא, “from that land,” הַהִוא follows הָאָרֶץ and agrees with it in gender, number, and definiteness. It points back to the land of Shinar in the preceding verse.
analysis.morphology: The definite article הַ precedes the third-person feminine singular pronoun הִוא, the Pentateuchal spelling of הִיא. The pronoun functions as a demonstrative.

analysis.evidence: The phrase מִן הָאָרֶץ הַהִוא (‘from that land’) identifies the place of departure.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: go out, depart from a place or someone’s presence

analysis.evidence: The repeated direct-object marker אֶת identifies Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah as the cities he built.
analysis.morphology: The conjunction וַ introduces יִּבֶן, the shortened third-person masculine singular Qal wayyiqtol of בָּנָה.

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּבֶן אֶת נִינְוֵה, “and he built Nineveh,” אֶת marks the city name נִינְוֵה as the direct object of וַיִּבֶן. The two following city names are each introduced by וְאֶת.
analysis.morphology: Direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a place-name article under the name’s own consonants, נינוה.
draft.definition: Nineveh, a city named among the places built in Genesis 10:11.
draft.evidence: Genesis 10:11 lists Nineveh as an object of “built.”

analysis.evidence: In וַיִּבֶן אֶת נִינְוֵה, “and he built Nineveh,” the name is the first in a list of places built. The context supports a city name and gives no basis for the proposed gloss “hearing; report” or a derivation from ניא.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with no prefix or suffix. The preceding אֶת is a separate word marking the direct object.

draft.change: Add Gen.10.11 as an example of the existing definite-object sense of word 0 in article 2t.
draft.definition: Introduces the particular person or thing a verb acts on, ordinarily a definite noun identified by the article, a name or a possessive suffix.
draft.evidence: In Gen.10.11, וְאֶת introduces the place name רְחֹבֹת עִיר as the second direct object of וַיִּבֶן.

analysis.evidence: וַיִּבֶן governs a list of places built. Between אֶת נִינְוֵה and וְאֶת כָּלַח, the marked וְאֶת introduces רְחֹבֹת עִיר as the second object of the same verb.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed conjunction וְ means “and.” אֶת is the unsuffixed direct-object particle.
analysis.sense: Marks רְחֹבֹת עִיר as a definite direct object of וַיִּבֶן, “he built.”

analysis.evidence: The repeated object marker אֶת sets וְאֶת רְחֹבֹת עִיר between Nineveh and Calah in the list of cities built. רְחֹבֹת and the following עִיר together name one city.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun with a feminine plural ending and no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Rehoboth, the first element of the place name Rehoboth-Ir

analysis.evidence: וְאֶת introduces רְחֹבֹת עִיר as one of the places built, between Nineveh and Calah. Within that name, עִיר supplies the sense “city” in “open places of a city.”
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular absolute noun with no prefix or suffix. It completes the place-name רְחֹבֹת עִיר.

draft.change: Add a place-name entry for כָּלַח with the gloss “Calah,” correcting the source gloss “wages.”
draft.definition: Calah, a city named in the account of the building of Nineveh and Rehoboth-Ir.
draft.evidence: In Genesis 10:11, וְאֶת כָּלַח completes the list of places governed by וַיִּבֶן.

analysis.evidence: The verse repeats the object marker before each place built. The final phrase וְאֶת כָּלַח adds “and Calah” to the list.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun. The preceding וְאֶת is a separate word that marks Calah as a coordinated direct object of וַיִּבֶן, “he built.”
analysis.sense: Calah, a city listed alongside Nineveh and Rehoboth-Ir.
